messages.subject: Possibility to profile a complex simulation
messages.subject_clean: Possibility to profile a complex simulation
messages.body_plain:
Does anyone have experience in profiling a complex simulation? Are there any profiling packages that work with simmer?

Is there some way to identify which part of a trajectory is run how many times or how long each element of a trajectory took to evaluate? I am interested in the real time to evaluate, not the simulation time. I am trying to optimize the runtime of my simulation, as it currently takes up to 48h, depending on parameters.

For example, I use renege_in to simulate a timeout for ~500k arrivals. Do i have a way to assess how long my out trajectory takes to evaluate in real time?

I usually use profviz to profile R code, but it seems to be only partially compatible to simmer, likely due to the way trajectories work.

Thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Possibility to profile a complex simulation
messages.subject_clean: [simmer-devel] Possibility to profile a complex simulation
messages.body_plain:
Usual tools for R profiling won't work, because the simulation engine
is basically a C++ program that calls back into the R session. For
this, you need a joint profiler, capable of following the execution
path across the R/C/C++ boundaries.

There aren't a lot of alternatives though. There is some work by
Kirill Müller in the r-prof organization [1], particularly the
jointprof package [2]. But I don't know the status of that project or
whether it works. It seems a bit abandoned. More recently, I came
across the xrprof project [3], which is in active development and
seems to implement some support for this too [4, 5].

Please, let us know if you succeed with any of these.

[1] https://github.com/r-prof
[2] https://github.com/r-prof/jointprof
[3] https://github.com/atheriel/xrprof
[4] https://github.com/atheriel/xrprof/issues/8
[5] https://github.com/atheriel/xrprof/issues/20

Iñaki

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 5 Mar 2021 at 01:25, N!P <cuys...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I cannot use a `branch` within a `mclapply(1:100, function(i) {}` correctly. I 'm having problem  with the env input.
>
> branch(function()

>     sum(get_server_count(env, paste0("server", 1:servers_Q))) ==  servers_Q-1, T,
>     trajectory() %>% set_capacity("queue",0)
>   ) %>%

That "env" must be a simmer environment, visible to that part of the
code when the simulation starts. See examples in [1] for a proper way
of doing this: the simulation is encapsulated in a simulate()
function, which is later called with mclapply.

[1] https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-aa-5g

--

messages.subject: Handling of retries / replicated arrivals.
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am looking for some inspiration to solve the following problem with Simmer in a somewhat efficient matter:

A predefined amount of arrivals exist, each with  an ID. Each ID ideally has a non fixed amount of entries (tries) each with different attributes corresponding to a temporal (this is a forward evolution, so absolute arrival times are increasing for each try within the ID) and spatial evolution.

Each arrival evaluates an acceptance function during the trajectory which is based on arrival attributes, resource attributes and current queue size, capacity size etc. If the function is accepted the trajectory goes forward and remaining arrivals tied to that ID should not be processed, or simply be rejected by some flag.
However if the acceptance function is rejected the next try tied to that ID should be allowed to be processed in the same manner. It is not a necessity that any try is accepted, so the individual "stop" condition is either an acceptance or running out of tries, i.e. every try being a leave / renege.

One line of enquiry was to clone arrivals on leave, renege etc. but as i undertand it's not possible to update the arrival time tied to the original data frame (i.e. essentially creating a delayed clone, and then having 1..n variables for each try in a single row in the initial data frame along with some try identifier to be updated).

The other idea is to seperate each try as a seperate arrival and then creating a giant global flagging variable outside the environment, which is to be updated once an acceptance has been made. Thus all subsequent tries will be denied. However with my limited knowledge this seems to create a lot of overhead, since we always have to evaluate every single arrival, leading to a worst case scenario.

Would appreciate any input / thoughts.

Best regards,
Christian
